title: Mind, Brain and AI
description: An interdisciplinary route through cognitive science, neuroscience and AI in twelve blocks, from what counts as an explanation of a mind to building, comparing and defending models of human behaviour and brains, with eight electives and explicit modelling methods. Following it never enrols you in its courses; each block is served by chosen units of the canonical courses, and a shared unit is studied and assessed once.

courses.note: Neuromatch as the spine, repaced for evening study; serves MBI-04 and MBI-08 and the model types of MBI-01.
Computational cognitive science read alongside; serves MBI-01 and MBI-04.
Models of human behaviour, beginning with the complete modelling loop of unit 1.
The research studio, when a question is ready.

blocks.title: Explaining Minds and Brains
blocks.centralQuestion: What counts as an explanation of a mind or brain?
blocks.entryLevel: Open entry; careful reading and willingness to argue about what a model claims.
requiredCoverage: The scope and limitations of an explanatory model
Competing accounts of the same observed behaviour
Experiments or observations that could discriminate between accounts
How a model can be useful without explaining everything
blocks.prerequisiteReasoning: None. It is the programme's foundation and is kept short so the other blocks can start alongside it; every later block returns to its distinctions.

courseMappings.contribution: Canonical course; its units are chosen after its introduction and examples are verified.
Prepared now: computational-level analysis and the distinction between a model and the evidence for it.
Prepared now: descriptive, mechanistic and normative ('what, how and why') models of neurons.

sourceShelf.note: Chapter 2: why model, capacities versus effects, Marr's levels kept apart from levels of organisation, and why models that predict need not explain.
W1D1 'what', 'how' and 'why' models, hands-on; W3D5 on causal versus correlational evidence.
A worked warning: standard neuroscience analyses fail to explain a microprocessor that is fully understood.
Lectures 1 and 2: Marr's levels and the problem of induction, already used by COG-201 unit 1.
Chapter 1, Reverse engineering the brain: the computational, algorithmic and implementation levels, with decision theory and resource rationality (a draft whose chapter files change in place).
Course notes 'Minds and Machines': Marr's levels and what a cognitive model looks like (draft notes of a course in progress).
MIT 9.13 (Kanwisher, 2019): the experimental-design assignment on the brain basis of intuitive physics, for how a question about the mind becomes an experiment.

activities.title: Two explanations of one result
activities.description: Given two explanations of a behavioural result, state each one's assumptions, the predictions on which they agree, and a condition on which they differ.

blocks.evidenceOfUnderstanding: A concise comparison that separates what is observed, what each model assumes, what it predicts, and what evidence would challenge it.
blocks.tutorGuidance: Ask which explanatory question the learner is answering. An implementation detail does not answer a question about purpose, and predictive fit does not prove a mechanism.
gaps: COG-100 has no prepared unit; prepared units in COG-201 and NEU-220 cover part of the ground.
What makes something a representation is not treated head-on (deliberately: no philosophy reading list).

blocks.title: Foundations of Neuroscience
blocks.centralQuestion: What biological components and experimental methods are needed to reason about brains?
blocks.entryLevel: Open entry. Mathematical maturity is not biological knowledge: the vocabulary and experimental context are taught properly, at a quantitative pace.
requiredCoverage: Cellular, circuit, systems and behavioural descriptions
Limitations and interpretation of different experimental methods
blocks.prerequisiteReasoning: None for NEU-101; NEU-201 adds biophysics and uses differential equations. It can run in parallel with MBI-01 and MBI-08, and should precede strong biological claims in MBI-11.

bridges.title: Quantitative neuron models
bridges.note: Integrate-and-fire and synapse models from computational neuroscience (in preparation).

courseMappings.contribution: Canonical course for components, anatomy and methods.
Canonical course for cellular and biophysical signalling.

sourceShelf.note: Medical-school depth on signalling, synapses, plasticity and organisation. Free to read, no licence: reference-only, so tutors cannot quote it.
MIT 9.40: the same biology for the mathematically confident (RC circuit, Nernst, Hodgkin-Huxley, dendrites, synapses), with videos.
What standard analyses can and cannot show.
W2D4 biological neuron models; W3D5 the logic of perturbation.

MIT 9.13 The Human Brain (Kanwisher, 2019): 17 recorded lectures with transcripts, weekly primary readings and reading responses on the functional organisation of the human brain; eight lectures have no recording or notes.

activities.title: One phenomenon at two scales
activities.description: Explain a neural phenomenon at two scales, connect each explanation to a type of observation, and identify what remains unresolved.

blocks.evidenceOfUnderstanding: The learner distinguishes the measured signal from the biological claim made about it and names a limitation of the evidence.
blocks.tutorGuidance: Do not let the course become a list of regions or an anatomy quiz; ask what a recording, image or lesion actually measured.
gaps: Recording, imaging and perturbation methods and their limits have no dedicated verified source; MIT 9.13 was verified from its index pages and one lecture's slides, and no lecture was watched.
The spine is reference-only, and neither canonical course has a prepared unit.

blocks.title: Cognitive Psychology
blocks.centralQuestion: How are perception, attention, memory, concepts and reasoning studied?
requiredCoverage: Limits of inferring internal processes from observed outcomes
blocks.prerequisiteReasoning: None. It supplies the tasks that MBI-04, MBI-05 and MBI-11 model and measure, so it is best started early, but it does not have to finish first.

courseMappings.contribution: Canonical course.
Rational models of categorisation connect the concepts topic to computational modelling (in preparation).

sourceShelf.note: Researcher-written modules on attention, memory, categories and concepts, language, judgement and perception.
Lectures 12 to 16: prototype, exemplar and Bayesian accounts of categorisation, and the number game, as tasks with competing explanations.
Computational accounts of concepts, causal reasoning and social cognition (reference-only).

activities.title: Separating two accounts
activities.description: Design a comparison that separates two accounts of performance on a cognitive task.

blocks.evidenceOfUnderstanding: The learner identifies the manipulation, the outcome, the competing predictions, plausible confounds and the limits of interpretation.
blocks.tutorGuidance: Connect each task to later computational modelling without implying that every psychological question already has one accepted model.
gaps: No working-memory source yet (MIT 9.00SC and 9.65 were opened and are the next candidates); reasoning is thin; COG-101 has no prepared unit.

blocks.title: Statistical Learning and Computational Inference
blocks.centralQuestion: How do observations constrain a computational model?
blocks.entryLevel: Probability at first-course level; the mathematics department's analysis and probability routes are available but not required.
blocks.prerequisiteReasoning: Probability is the only hard requirement. The block reuses prepared units from NEU-220, COG-201 and CSA-210 instead of repeating them under three headings, and its complete modelling loop is COG-260 unit 1.

courseMappings.contribution: Canonical course for machine-learning foundations.
Canonical course for probabilistic modelling and Bayesian inference.
Canonical course; shares its inference units with MBI-05.
Prepared now: least squares, likelihood, bootstrap uncertainty and model selection.
Prepared now: Bayesian inference over an inspectable hypothesis space.
Prepared now: training, validation and held-out evaluation.
Unit 1: the complete simulate, fit, recover and evaluate loop.

sourceShelf.note: From Bayes' rule to MCMC, posterior predictive checks, cross-validation and hierarchical models (R and Stan).
W1D2: least squares, likelihood, bootstrap, bias-variance, cross-validation in Python.
Bayesian data analysis of cognitive models and the Bayesian Occam's razor.
The modelling loop: simulate, fit, check parameter and model recovery, validate; the two-armed bandit example that COG-260 unit 1 and its laboratory follow (rules numbered in heading order).
Lecture 9 slides: model fitting, estimation and comparison (Spring 2024 archive; MIT-licensed repository).

activities.title: Inspectable generative model
activities.description: Specify and simulate a modest model, fit it, investigate recovery on synthetic data, and evaluate prediction on appropriate held-out data.

blocks.evidenceOfUnderstanding: A short report explaining the objective or likelihood, the fitted parameters and their uncertainty, the recovery results, the evaluation split and a limitation.
blocks.tutorGuidance: Not 'fit a regression and display accuracy': ask how the assumptions, the simulated observations, the fitted parameters and the predictions relate.
gaps: CSA-201, CSA-220 and COG-210 have no prepared unit; the block is taught today through mapped prepared units, including COG-260 unit 1.
Identifiability is taught through parameter and model recovery (Wilson and Collins); formal identifiability analysis has no source yet.

blocks.title: Measurement and Experimental Design
blocks.centralQuestion: What does a measurement or experiment actually justify?
blocks.entryLevel: Basic statistics; MBI-04's inference units help.
blocks.prerequisiteReasoning: Shares COG-210 with MBI-04; can begin once basic estimation and uncertainty are familiar. Applications to games or talent discovery are optional examples; the block works as measurement science on its own.

courseMappings.contribution: Canonical course for design, randomisation and uncertainty.
Canonical course for reliability, validity and invariance.
Prepared now: what a held-out evaluation does and does not justify.
Unit 3 (outlined): what a fitted parameter measures, reliability and generalisation.

sourceShelf.note: Operational definitions, reliability (test-retest, internal consistency, inter-rater), validity, random assignment, practice effects and counterbalancing.
Constructs and operationalisation, critically, with questions for transparent reporting (reference-only).
Measurement invariance by multi-group factor analysis, alignment and differential item functioning (advanced).
Reliabilities of seven classic tasks ranged from 0 to .82: the intraclass correlation, and why low variance between people helps experiments but harms individual differences.
Whether learning-model parameters generalise across three tasks done by the same 291 participants: only partly, and only between similar tasks.

activities.title: Task effect or individual difference
activities.description: Compare the evidence needed for an experimental task effect with the evidence needed to rank individuals or to track change within a person.

blocks.evidenceOfUnderstanding: A proposed study with a clear construct, operationalisation, sampling or repeated-measures plan, analysis and limitations.
blocks.tutorGuidance: Keep apart: improving at a particular task, a change in a measured score, a change in the construct of interest, and a claim that the measure is useful in an application.
gaps: Longitudinal change (change scores, growth models, regression to the mean) has no source yet; invariance is covered only at an advanced level.
Neither canonical course has a prepared unit, and the measurement method has no prepared unit.

blocks.title: Learning and Decision-Making
blocks.centralQuestion: How do people learn from experience and choose under uncertainty?
blocks.entryLevel: Probability and the idea of a value; MBI-04 helps with fitting.
blocks.prerequisiteReasoning: Shares reinforcement-learning foundations with MBI-10 through CSA-230, taught once. The algorithm's definition and the empirical claim that a person uses it are kept apart throughout.

courseMappings.contribution: Canonical course for learning and choice models.
Canonical course for reinforcement learning, shared with MBI-10.
Unit 1 compares a learning model with a heuristic and a baseline on choice data.
Unit 1 compares model-based and cached strategies; units 2 and 5 (outlined) treat the two-step task and Dyna.

sourceShelf.note: Chapter 2 on bandits and soft-max action preferences, sections 6.4 to 6.6 on temporal-difference control including Q-learning, chapter 8 on planning and learning, and section 14.6 on habitual and goal-directed behaviour. CC BY-NC-ND: imported for private study only and never shared in adapted form.
Comparing learning models on choice data, as COG-260 unit 1 does.
Chapter 10, Learning to predict: classical conditioning, the Rescorla-Wagner model, temporal-difference learning and the dopamine prediction-error account (draft).
Recurrent networks fitted to choices against Q-learning baselines, compared by leave-one-subject-out prediction.
W3D4 reinforcement learning; W3D2 Bayesian decisions.
Rational process models, for bounded rationality.

activities.title: Two learning accounts
activities.description: Compare at least two learning or choice models on labelled synthetic data or permitted public data.

blocks.evidenceOfUnderstanding: The learner explains why the models make different predictions, where the data distinguish them, and where they do not.
blocks.tutorGuidance: A model-free algorithm fitting choices well is not evidence that a person runs that algorithm.
gaps: No verified source yet for choice models as statistical models (logit, random utility, sequential sampling).
COG-230 and CSA-230 have no prepared unit; COG-260 unit 1 and COG-250 unit 1 carry the block's choice-learning and planning material today.

blocks.title: Neural Networks and Representations
blocks.centralQuestion: How do networks learn representations, and how should those representations be investigated?
blocks.entryLevel: Linear algebra, calculus and Python; no expensive GPU is needed to start.
requiredCoverage: Limits of claims about biological similarity
blocks.prerequisiteReasoning: CSA-210 is a launch course and the block's canonical course; units 1 and 2 are prepared. It precedes MBI-10 and the representation side of MBI-11.

courseMappings.contribution: Evidence discipline, gradients, networks, generalisation, attention and representation learning.

sourceShelf.note: The course's existing spine.

Understanding Deep Learning (PDF of February 2026): chapters 3 (shallow networks), 7 (gradients and initialisation), 12 (transformers) and 19 (reinforcement learning), with MIT-licensed notebooks. CC BY-NC-ND: adapted text and figures are never shared.
W1D3: representational geometry, RSA with bootstrap model comparison and dynamical similarity; W1D2 tasks as cost functions.

activities.title: A small model and an ablation
activities.description: Train a small model, examine a representation, and compare a baseline or an ablation.

blocks.evidenceOfUnderstanding: The learner explains the objective, what changed during training, what the comparison establishes and what it does not.
blocks.tutorGuidance: An attractive embedding plot is not evidence that a model 'thinks like a brain'.
gaps: Units 3 to 10 of CSA-210 are outlined, not prepared.
CKA or CCA style representation comparison has no source yet.

blocks.title: Systems and Computational Neuroscience
blocks.centralQuestion: How can computation help explain neural systems and behaviour?
blocks.entryLevel: Calculus, linear algebra and Python; MBI-02 for the biology.
blocks.prerequisiteReasoning: NEU-220 is a launch course with four prepared units; NEU-210 supplies systems organisation. Synthetic demonstrations are kept distinct from real neural data, and dataset provenance is recorded.

courseMappings.contribution: Canonical course for systems organisation.
Fitting, encoding and decoding, population structure and dynamics.

sourceShelf.note: The course's existing spine.
Spike trains, receptive fields, PCA, recurrent networks and integrators, with videos.
Sensory and motor systems for systems organisation (reference-only).
Microcircuits and macrocircuits days as the bridge to NeuroAI.
Chapter 10, section 7: the neural architecture of reinforcement learning (dopamine prediction errors, stimulus representation, three-factor plasticity) (draft).

activities.title: A modest neural-modelling analysis
activities.description: Reproduce a modest neural-modelling analysis and explain an assumption, a baseline and a failure case.

blocks.evidenceOfUnderstanding: An interpretable analysis with a written explanation, not a notebook whose cells merely ran.
blocks.tutorGuidance: Ask why the model behaves as it does and what the synthetic data can and cannot say about real neurons.
gaps: NEU-210 has no prepared unit; NEU-220 units 6 and 8 are outlined, not prepared; no population-dynamics reading beyond Neuromatch.

blocks.title: Planning and Structured Cognition
blocks.centralQuestion: How do minds represent structure and solve problems across several steps?
blocks.entryLevel: MBI-06's idea of learned value helps; the first unit introduces what it needs.
requiredCoverage: Distinguishing an observed result from the strategy that produced it
blocks.prerequisiteReasoning: Builds on the model-free versus model-based contrast of MBI-06 but does not require MBI-06 to be finished; the causal and program-like topics connect to COG-201.

bridges.title: Causal and program-like models
bridges.note: Causal learning and causal theories (in preparation).

courseMappings.contribution: Canonical course: unit 1 (planning strategies and transfer) is prepared; units 2 to 8 are outlined.

sourceShelf.note: Section 8.1 on models and planning, Dyna in section 8.2, the blocking and shortcut mazes of section 8.3 (which compare Dyna-Q with Dyna-Q+), and section 14.6 on habitual and goal-directed behaviour: the basis of COG-250 unit 1.
The two-step task: after a rare transition that is rewarded, model-free learners tend to repeat and model-based learners to switch (author manuscript; read on PubMed Central, not importable).
Planning by tree search with pruning below large losses; its model comparison is in-sample.
Cognitive maps: latent learning and spatial orientation. Reference-only; the words 'shortcut' and 'short cut' do not occur in it.
Chapters 1 and 4 on resource rationality and costly inference, for the bounded-rational accounts of COG-250 unit 8 (draft).
Rational process models and the sampling hypothesis (reference-only).

activities.title: Two planners and a transfer test
activities.description: Compare two planning strategies on a controlled task with an explicit state space and test what happens in a transfer condition.

blocks.evidenceOfUnderstanding: The learner specifies the strategies, their assumptions, predicted behaviour, costs or constraints, and the interpretation of the transfer result.
blocks.tutorGuidance: Longer tasks do not automatically give better evidence about planning; ask which observations distinguish the candidate strategies.
gaps: COG-250 unit 1 is prepared and units 2 to 5 and 8 are outlined with verified sources; hierarchical and compositional representations, analogy and relational reasoning have no verified source yet.

blocks.title: Modern AI
blocks.centralQuestion: How do modern learning systems acquire, deploy and test capabilities?
blocks.entryLevel: MBI-07; for the full implementation route, substantial programming and systems experience (Stanford CS336's stated prerequisites). A conceptual route is offered to learners not yet ready for it.
blocks.prerequisiteReasoning: Shares reinforcement learning with MBI-06 through CSA-230. Fast-moving material is taken from dated primary sources; nothing is called the latest.

courseMappings.contribution: Canonical course for language modelling from scratch.
Canonical course for agents, evaluation and reliable applications.
Canonical course for reinforcement learning, shared with MBI-06.

sourceShelf.note: The conceptual route: transformers, pretraining, instruction tuning and preference learning without a GPU (reference-only; the agents chapter is not yet written).
The advanced implementation route, with its stated prerequisites and GPU-hour budgets; its evaluation lecture suits both routes (reference-only).

Reinforcement learning for reasoning: R1-Zero trained by reinforcement learning from the base model, group relative policy optimisation, rule-based and model-based rewards, and the authors' account of limitations and reward hacking. The Nature version is CC BY but not importable from its hosts; the arXiv version grants no reuse.
A learned world model with critic and actor learning, evaluated on benchmarks, Minecraft, ablations and scaling; the CC BY arXiv preprint is the working copy.
Chapter 12, Transformers, as the prerequisite chapter for the conceptual route.

activities.title: A component or a careful critique
activities.description: Reproduce a small component or critically analyse an accessible experiment with explicit baselines and limitations.

blocks.evidenceOfUnderstanding: A component that works with a stated baseline, or a critique that names the evaluation, the contamination and shift risks, and what the result does not show.
blocks.tutorGuidance: Not API wrappers or prompt tips; a full-scale training run is never required to show serious understanding.
gaps: None of the three canonical courses has a prepared unit; contamination and distribution shift are covered only by CS336's evaluation lecture.

blocks.title: Models of Human Behaviour and NeuroAI
blocks.centralQuestion: How should models of human behaviour be built, compared and interpreted?
blocks.entryLevel: MBI-04 (likelihood and fitting); MBI-07 for the neural-network models.
blocks.prerequisiteReasoning: Every predictive exercise states its information contract first. Random trial splits never stand in for transfer to unseen people or tasks; where a dataset cannot support an evaluation, the course says so.

courseMappings.contribution: Canonical course: unit 1 (the complete modelling loop) is prepared; units 2 to 8 are outlined.
Canonical course for NeuroAI.

sourceShelf.note: Verified as current (CC BY 4.0); entry requires the computational neuroscience and deep learning courses or their equivalent.

Centaur and Psych-101: held-out participants within the trained experiments, then separate generalisation tests, and a summary that outruns one non-significant panel; read with Oh and Gobet and the published critiques. The arXiv preprint is the working copy.
Fourteen small models (135M to 14B parameters) on Centaur's splits: scale barely matters in distribution and does out of distribution; masking stimuli and feedback removes most of what was learned.
The procedure behind COG-260 unit 1.
The dataset behind Centaur (Apache-2.0, about 859 MB; not imported; its gated test set may not be redistributed).
Probabilistic models of cognition for the classical side.

activities.title: Three models, one contract
activities.description: Compare an interpretable cognitive model, a simple predictive baseline and another appropriately scoped model on a modest behavioural task.

blocks.evidenceOfUnderstanding: The learner explains the evaluation setting, the model assumptions, the information available, the performance with its uncertainty, and the transfer limits.
blocks.tutorGuidance: Success on a game dataset does not establish general cognitive measurement, hiring validity, medical usefulness or accurate prediction of an unobserved person.
gaps: NEU-230 has no prepared unit, and the plasticity-as-optimisation chapter of Gershman's draft textbook is known by title only.
COG-260 unit 1 is prepared; units 2 to 8 are outlined, and unit 8's privacy and application-claims coverage has no verified source yet.

blocks.title: Independent Research Studio
blocks.centralQuestion: Can the learner investigate a question and defend what the evidence supports?
blocks.entryLevel: At least one modelling block (usually MBI-04 or MBI-11) and one subject block.
requiredCoverage: An optional oral discussion or defence
blocks.prerequisiteReasoning: Comes last because it uses the others, but a small conceptual or replication project can start early. No participant recruitment, outreach, publication or private business data is ever automated.

courseMappings.contribution: Canonical course; the project workflow is designed, not yet built.

sourceShelf.note: Reproducibility, version control, environments, data management, testing and a project checklist.
A preregistration template for applying cognitive models, with a worked example (not importable: hosted on PubMed Central).
Rule 10 on reporting model-based analyses: the standard a project report is judged against.

activities.title: A defensible investigation
activities.description: Reduce an overlarge question to a defensible investigation, run it, and report what the evidence supports, including negative results.

blocks.evidenceOfUnderstanding: A report whose claims match its evidence, with limitations and, where they occur, well-explained negative results.
blocks.tutorGuidance: Help shrink the question without pretending a toy exercise answers the whole research problem; reward a clear limitation.
gaps: The research-project workflow (proposal, provenance, artefacts, report) is specified but not built.
No source yet on reporting negative results or on notebook practice.

electives.note: Emotional and motivational influences on learning, choice and effort.
Mental-state inference, coordination and strategic interaction.
Measurement models and validation beyond COG-220.
Meta-learning, adaptation and leakage-aware task splits.

methods.title: Parameter recovery
learnerShould: Investigate more than one convenient setting
Examine the effect of data quantity or task conditions
Report uncertainty, systematic errors and limitations

methods.title: Model recovery and model comparison
learnerShould: Apply an explicitly chosen comparison procedure
methods.evidence: A confusion matrix with an interpretation that treats a failure to distinguish models as a result.

methods.title: Predictive and simulation checks
learnerShould: Compare predictions with relevant observed or simulated patterns
Use posterior predictive checks where the Bayesian material supports them
methods.evidence: A held-out comparison with a baseline and a stated validation question; never the bare phrase 'validated model'.

methods.title: Measurement reliability and validity
learnerShould: Distinguish an average experimental effect from ranking people
Distinguish within-person change and practice effects
Separate the interpretation of a score from its proposed use

methods.evidence: A study proposal whose measurement claims match the evidence it would collect.

methods.title: Longitudinal and transfer evaluation
learnerShould: Distinguish held-out trials, people, tasks and later periods
State the information available at prediction time

paperSeminar.title: Mind, Brain and AI paper seminar
paperSeminar.description: A fixed, bounded list of papers read one at a time, each with a structured report and an optional small analysis. It is not a feed: papers enter the list only by a deliberate edit, and the list never exceeds its bound.

papers.focus: What each rule protects against, and which rule your own last analysis skipped.
Why a robust task effect can be a poor measure of individual differences.

Which generalisation the evaluation tests (held-out participants within experiments, then separate tests), where the summary outruns one reported panel, and which application claims it does not support.
What it means that small models match a large one in distribution but not out of distribution, and what the ablations remove.
What reasoning-oriented reinforcement learning was trained with which rewards, what the authors report as its limitations, and whether its evaluation guards against contamination.
What a learned world model buys, against which baselines, at what compute.
